Learning Objectives
Review the background and common presentation of chordoma.
Discuss the management of chordoma.
Describe the background and common presentation of adamantinoma.
Explain the management of adamantinoma.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Chordoma
Slow-growing malignant bone tumor arising from notochordal rests and occurring in the
spinal axis
Occurs in adult patients (>40 years)

Lesions at the base of skull present earlier than sacral lesions.
Adamantinoma
Unusual, rare, slow-growing malignant bone tumor often found in the tibia (Figure 1)
Most are similar to osteofibrous dysplasia but not a direct result
Figure 1 Images show adamantinoma of the tibia. A, AP radiograph of the tibia of a 38-year-old
woman reveals demonstrates multiple diaphyseal lucent lesions separated by sclerotic bone. The
lesions have a bubbly appearance consistent with adamantinoma. B, Gross specimen from a
different patient shows lesions that expand the bone in the tibia and fibula. C, Histologic image of
adamantinoma shows nests of epithelial cells in a fibrous stroma. (Reproduced from Weber KL:
Malignant bone tumors, Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1560-1586.)
Epidemiology
Chordoma
Male-to-female ratio = 3:1 (most apparent in sacral lesions)
Occurs in adult patients (>40 years).
Sacral lesions are more common than lesions in other parts of spine.
Adamantinoma
Slightly more common in males than females
Patients generally are aged 20 to 40 years.
Fewer than 300 cases reported in the literature

Etiology
Chordoma
Chordoma is thought to result from residual notochordal cells that eventually undergo
neoplastic change.
Brachyury gene duplication is a major susceptibility mutation in familial chordoma. No clear
marker for sporadic forms is known.
Adamantinoma
Controversial whether adamantinoma evolves from osteofibrous dysplasia; most believe it
does not.
As a result of epithelial nests, no proven origin of etiology
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Chordoma
Insidious onset of low back or sacral pain
Frequently misdiagnosed as osteoarthritis, nerve impingement, or disk herniation
Infrequent distal motor/sensory loss because most lesions occur below S1.
Bowel/bladder symptoms occur regularly.
50% can be identified on a careful rectal examination. (transrectal biopsy should not be
performed.)
50% occur in the sacrococcygeal region, 35% occur in the spheno-occipital region, and 15%
occur in the mobile spine.
Adamantinoma
Pain of variable duration and intensity is the major symptom.
Occasional tibial deformity or a mass
Tenderness over the subcutaneous tibial border
History of preceding trauma is common (30% to 60%).
Approximately 80% to 90% of lesions occur in the tibial diaphysis.
Synchronous involvement of the ipsilateral fibula in 10% to 50% of patients
Imaging Studies
Radiography

Chordoma
Chordomas occur in the midline, consistent with prior notochord location.
Findings on plain radiographs of the sacrum are subtle because of overlying bowel gas.
Radiographic differential diagnosis includes chondrosarcoma, multiple myeloma, metastatic
disease, giant cell tumor, and lymphoma (Table 1).

Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020,

Adamantinoma
Classic radiographic appearance is multiple, well-circumscribed lucent defects, usually with
one dominant defect that can expand the bone locally (Figure 1, A).
Sclerotic bone between defects

So-called soap bubble appearance
Lesions can be intracortical or intramedullary, with occasional (10%) soft-tissue mass.
No periosteal reaction but involves the periosteum, which distinguishes it from osteofibrous
dysplasia
Computed Tomography
Chordoma
Cross-sectional imaging via CT or MRI required (Figure 2, A through C)
Figure 2 Images show chordoma of the sacrum in a 66-year-old man. A, Axial CT scan of the
sacrum shows a destructive lesion with an anterior soft-tissue mass containing calcifications.
B, Axial MRI of the sacrum shows soft-tissue extension anteriorly and toward the left pelvic
sidewall. C, Sagittal T1-weighted MRI of the sacrum shows the lesion at S3 and below. Note
that the anterior extension abuts the rectum. D, Low-power histologic image of the lesion
shows a tumor lobule surrounded by fibrous tissue. E, Higher power histologic image of the
lesion shows the physaliferous cells of a chordoma with a bubbly appearance to the
cytoplasm. (Reproduced from Weber KL: Malignant bone tumors, Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS

CT reveals areas of calcification within the lesion.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Chordoma
Cross-sectional imaging via CT or MRI required (Figure 2, A through C).
MRI (low signal intensity on T1-weighted images; high signal intensity on T2-weighted images)
defines the extent of the frequent anterior soft-tissue mass and bony involvement (usually
involves multiple sacral levels).
Pathology
Chordoma
Grossly, chordoma appears lobulated and jellylike, with tumor tracking along the nerve roots.
The signature cell is the physaliferous cell, which contains intracellular vacuoles and appears
bubbly as a result of cytoplasmic mucus droplets (Figure 2, D and E).
Lobules of the tumor are separated by fibrous septa.
Physaliferous cells are keratin positive, which differentiates this tumor from
chondrosarcoma.
Weakly S100 positive
Adamantinoma
Nests of epithelial cells in a benign fibrous stroma (Figure 1, C)
Epithelial cells are columnar in appearance and keratin positive.
Epithelial cells are bland without mitosis.
The epithelial cells distinguish adamantinoma from osteofibrous dysplasia.
Differential Diagnosis
Chordoma
Chondrosarcoma and metastatic carcinoma

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Chordoma
Patients with diffusely metastatic disease can be treated palliatively; otherwise the disease
should be managed surgically.
Adamantinoma
Nonsurgical management is not advocated.
Techniques/Procedures
Chordoma
Embolization can decrease the size of the mass and improve symptoms.
Radiation therapy can be used for palliative purposes.
Adamantinoma
Nonsurgical management is not advocated.
Surgical Management
Indications
Chordoma
Almost all patients will be treated surgically unless they have a very small tumor that would
require considerable morbidity.
Patients with a large tumor require complex surgical preparation and plans to fully remove
the tumor.
Adamantinoma
Almost all patients undergo surgical treatment.
Techniques/Procedures

Preoperative Planning
Chordoma
MRI and CT are performed to verify bone and soft-tissue extension of the mass.
Pulmonary imaging should be performed preoperatively to verify the absence of metastatic
disease.
Adamantinoma
MRI and radiographs are obtained preoperatively to determine the extent of bone and soft-
tissue involvement.
Surgical Approaches
Chordoma
The main treatment option is wide surgical resection.
Local recurrence is common (50%) and directly related to the surgical margin achieved.
To achieve a satisfactory wide margin, surgeons may need to sacrifice involved nerve roots,
viscera, etc.
Radiation therapy (proton preferred) can be used as an adjunct for locally recurrent disease,
for positive margins, or for primary management of inoperable tumors (protons or photons).
High-dose proton radiation therapy alone (70 Gy) is associated with reasonable short-term
local control and can be performed in patients with metastatic disease or who have a small
tumor that would require considerable morbidity with resection.
Chemotherapy is not effective and currently is not indicated.
Adamantinoma
Standard of care is wide surgical resection.
Chemotherapy and radiation therapy are not indicated.
Local recurrence is more common if adequate margins are not achieved.
Given the diaphyseal location, common reconstruction involves the use of intercalary
allograft or bone transport.
Outcomes
Chordoma
Chordoma metastasizes late to the lungs and, occasionally, to the bone and requires long-
term follow-up (20 years).
Long-term survival is 25% to 50%, partly because of local progression.

Adamantinoma
Late metastasis to the lungs, bones, and lymph nodes in 10% to 30% of patients
Requires long-term follow-up
A case series from 2000 described an 87% survival rate at 10 years1
